name: The Permanent Income Hypothesis
statement: People base consumption mainly on their expected long-run average income, not on temporary fluctuations in current income.
meaning: Friedman argued that measured income splits into a permanent component (the stable, anticipated part) and a transitory component (temporary windfalls or shortfalls). Consumption tracks permanent income closely, while transitory income is mostly saved or borrowed against rather than spent. This explains why consumption is much smoother than income over time.
mechanism: Consumers estimate their expected lifetime earning power and set consumption proportional to it. A one-time bonus, tax rebate, or bad harvest is treated as transitory and largely absorbed into saving or debt rather than driving proportional spending, so the short-run marginal propensity to consume out of current income looks much lower than out of permanent income.

examples.text: Studies of the 2008 US stimulus tax rebates (Johnson, Parker & Souleles) found households spent only a modest share of the one-time rebate immediately, consistent with rebates being treated as transitory income.

A worker who receives an unexpected bonus does not proportionally raise spending that month; the hypothesis predicts the extra income is largely saved and its effect on consumption spread across future periods.
Households with highly variable income, such as commission-based or seasonal earners, tend to keep consumption stable by saving in high-income periods and drawing down savings in low-income periods.

whyItMatters: The hypothesis reshaped how economists and policymakers think about fiscal stimulus, predicting that temporary tax rebates have weaker effects on spending than permanent tax cuts, and it underlies modern consumption-smoothing models in macroeconomics and public finance.
limits: It assumes consumers can freely borrow and save to smooth consumption, but many households face liquidity constraints. Empirical work (Flavin, 1981) found consumption shows "excess sensitivity" to predictable current-income changes, contradicting a strict version of the hypothesis.
misreadings: It does not claim windfalls have zero effect on spending — only that their effect is smaller and more spread over time than a naive one-for-one response to current income would suggest.
origin: Developed by American economist Milton Friedman, published in his 1957 book "A Theory of the Consumption Function."
